t: Gandhi worked out his method of nonviolent resistance, satyagraha, during 21 years in South Africa and brought it to India in 1915.
As leader of the Indian National Congress from 1921 he turned the demand for self-rule into mass campaigns, among them the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India movement of 1942.
India became independent in August 1947 through a partition he opposed, and he was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist on 30 January 1948.
dyk: As a law student in London Gandhi was too shy to read out his own defence of a fellow member at a committee meeting of the London Vegetarian Society, so the president had another member read it for him.
ev: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi is born in Porbandar on the Kathiawar Peninsula
After three years in London he is called to the bar at the age of 22 and returns to India
He sails for South Africa to act as lawyer in a merchant's lawsuit and stays for 21 years
At a mass meeting in Johannesburg he adopts satyagraha, nonviolent protest, against the Transvaal's registration law
He returns to India at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale and joins the Indian National Congress
He leads the Salt March from Ahmedabad to Dandi to break the British salt laws
He calls on the British to Quit India and is arrested and held for two years
Nathuram Godse shoots him dead at Birla House in Delhi

f.born: 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula, into a Gujarati Hindu Modh Bania family; third son of Karamchand Gandhi, dewan of Porbandar state, and Putlibai
f.died: 30 January 1948 in Delhi, shot three times in the chest by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist, in the garden of Birla House on his way to a prayer meeting
f.role: Barrister, called to the bar in 1891; lawyer and campaigner for Indian civil rights in South Africa, 1893–1914; leader of the Indian National Congress from 1921; resigned his Congress membership in 1934
f.known: Nonviolent resistance (satyagraha); the campaign for Indian independence; the Salt March of 1930; the call on the British to Quit India in 1942; campaigns against untouchability; fasts as political protest; the book Hind Swaraj (1909)
